doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Introduction; how San Francisco has changed since the 1920s
summary: Rowe opens the interview; Watkins describes ferries, bridges, districts, the Sunset's sand dunes and the postwar building boom.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I am filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive today in San Francisco and I’m very pleased to have Earl Watkins with me.

And your name seems to be synonymous with music here in San Francisco as I discovered in talking to a number of people out here on the phone — they always mentioned your name. “You better talk to Earl” they said. So it’s a great pleasure to be here. I have a feeling that San Francisco has changed a lot since your youth.

Well yes. I’m a native born San Franciscan, I was born in 1920, January the 29th, and there have been many, many, many changes. Everything. Our skyline has changed, it’s been Manhattanized, our transportation system, which used to be the best in the country, we’re having problems with it. We went from all electric streetcars and cable cars and we went to buses and we do have light rail now but it’s in trouble, our municipal railway. We have an underground, which we never had before, then we have of course the BART, that’s here of course — well I’m getting ahead of myself. We have two bridges which we didn’t have before. When I was growing up we had ferry boats, yeah, we rode the ferry. There was a ferry to Sausalito, there was a ferry to Oakland, there was a ferry to Berkeley, and there was a ferry that ran to Richmond and from Richmond there was a ferry that ran over to San Rafael. So now we have the Golden Gate Bridge, which leads you into Marin County, we have the Bay Bridge from San Francisco to Oakland, then we have another bridge from Richmond to San Rafael, the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge. And now also we have a San Mateo Bridge, that’s a bridge from Hayward to San Mateo. But that bridge — I think that’s been there — for as long as I can remember that’s been there. Then they have another one they call the Dunbarton Bridge. And it runs, you go further south past Hayward and it’s down near Mountain View and then you cross over and it’s more — I guess it’s more like a land bridge more than above the water. So now also we have different districts here. We have the — well naturally downtown, the Nob Hill, we have the South of Market, you’ve got the Western Addition — that’s where I

grew up — and you’ve got the Richmond District, that’s going out to the beach say from Presidio Avenue west and that’s on the north side of Geary Blvd. Then you have the Sunset District. Now the Sunset District would be beyond our deYoung museum in the past, that would be going west, and on the opposite side of the park, the south side of the park, all of that area. Now that area, when I was growing up, was sand dunes. They had sand dunes. You had streets but you had sand dunes. And when you’d take people out, if you were going to teach someone how to drive a vehicle, you’d take them out there to the sand dunes, so if the car got out of a control why there would be no damage. Of course after World War II then there was this big building boom, and so this fella Doelger, he built — he developed the Sunset and also the area where San Francisco State is, Stonestown, Daly City. So there’s just been all kinds of change. And of course our population — the population, it’s not necessarily San Francisco although we’ve had a big increase here, but the Bay area see, now San Francisco is very small, we’re like on the tip of the peninsula and we can only go—
Right. You can only go so far.

Yeah you can only go up, like New York, huh? And the traffic. Now before, when I was growing up, very few people had cars. Very few of the people that I knew and my family knew, and also the people who were considered to be the business people, maybe corporate owners at that time. They had chauffeurs. Chauffeurs was a big thing. My dad was a chauffeur.
